title: Differences in training characteristics of recreational endurance runners by race distance - results from the NURMI Study (Step 2)
authors: Knechtle B, Tanous D, Thuany M, Motevalli M, Wirnitzer G, Leitzmann C, et al.
population: Recreational runners preferring 10 km, half-marathon or marathon/ultra, web survey (German-speaking countries)
findings: The abstract states 154 recreational runners; the full text reports 317 completed surveys and 245 analysed after data clearance (91 10-km, 89 half-marathon, 65 marathon/ultra), so the sample size is inconsistent within the paper.

10 km runners trained the least distance and time in every period reported (Table 3); weekly volume ranged from 18.5 km and 1.0 h (transition/recovery, Period A) to 31.8 km and 4.78 h (competition-trial condition), with a median of 2-3 sessions per week.
Main competitive period (Period C), 10 km group (mean +/- SD): 26.0 +/- 20.5 km, 3.57 +/- 2.8 h, 3 sessions per week; half-marathon 27.8 km and 3.8 h; marathon/ultra 47.3 km, 6.48 h and 4 sessions.
The article reports no longest-run or long-run variable for any group; the reported per-day figure for the 10 km group in Period C is 8.79 km and 0.38 h.
limitations: Self-reported survey; standard deviations are about as large as the means; hours imply roughly 7-8 min/km, suggesting hours include non-running training or are overestimated; the per-day hours (0.38 h) do not reconcile with weekly hours divided by sessions (about 71 min), so session length cannot be derived; sample size inconsistent between abstract and tables; goal-distance groups are self-reported preferences.
implications: Typical recreational 10 km runners report about 3 sessions and 3.5-4.8 h per week (self-reported, high variance), which supports a medium tier around 3-5 h/week with 3 run days.
At 2-3 sessions and under 3 h/week, a long run is necessarily a large share of the week; cap the share, not only the minutes, at low volume. Per-session length cannot be inferred from this source.
